Designer pigs

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
.......scientists grow replacement organs in pigs.

Unique Selling Point:
New medical advance that could alleviate the massive donor organ shortage world wide

Summary:
Each year, hundreds of thousands of people join organ donor lists hoping to get a replacement liver or kidney. But very few get transplants. There are just not enough organs to go around, and it is getting worse every day -- also in South Africa. For example there are 50 000 people in need of dialysis because of renal failure. Only 8000 can get dialysis. the other 42 000 are sent home to die. There are no kidneys for transplants. One way to fill the gap between need and supply would be to grow the organs another way — in animals. Scientists are now working to create designer pigs that could grow organs for human bodies. US scientists are the closest yet to creating genetically modified pigs with organs that can be safely transplanted into humans.


Further information:
In South Africa the lack of organs for transplantation is also serious. Shortcomings in the law and widespread ignorance about organ donation are contributing to a major shortage of organs for transplant in South Africa. The problem is particularly severe among patients suffering from kidney failure, thousands of whom are turned away from the dialysis units of public hospitals every year.

“Organ and tissue donation is not a priority for government and there is a huge need to spread the message about it in communities,” said Prof Magda Slabbert, an expert in medical law at Unisa’s College of Law, in a presentation on 1 March during the university’s annual Research & Innovation Week.

Only two public hospitals in Gauteng were willing to provide statistics on the situation at their dialysis units, but their experience is illuminating, according to Slabbert.

“They each show away approximately 500 patients a month. That’s 1 000 people who are shown the door per month and who actually go home to die because they cannot dialyse themselves.”

Kidney failure is becoming chronic in South Africa, she said, mainly as a result of the growth in diabetes. Without access to dialysis or a kidney transplant, patients with kidney failure face a bleak future.

And there are many thousands of people in dire need of other organs – heart, liver, pancreas, lung, etc.

One way to fill the gap between need and supply would be to grow the organs another way — in animals.

Scientists are now working to create designer pigs that could grow organs for human bodies.
US scientists are the closest yet to creating genetically modified pigs with organs that can be safely transplanted into humans.

The researchers identified and eliminated 25 porcine endogenous retroviruses (PERVS) hidden in the pigs’ DNA that can trigger organs to be rejected by the human immune system, thereby overcoming one of the biggest barriers in interspecies transplant or “xenotransplantation.”

Our study highlighted the value of PERV inactivation to prevent cross-species viral transmission and demonstrated the successful production of PERV-inactivated animals to address the safety concern in clinical xenotransplantation,” Luhan Yang (Harvard university) and colleagues.
The researchers say preventing the rejection of pig organs is a huge challenge, but that these pigs are the most genetically modified animals far. If xenotransplantation can be made safe, it has the potential to prevent the thousands of people in need of transplants having to wait so long to receive an organ.

As reported in Science, the team used the gene-editing technology CRISPR to eliminate the viruses in 37 pigs. This game-changing technology involves a piece of “guide RNA” binding to a sequence of viral DNA and then guiding an enzyme to cut it at specific sites, so that DNA parts can be removed or added.

Next, using the same cloning technology that created Dolly the sheep, the researchers inserted the modified genetic material into pigs’ eggs to create embryos, which resulted in the birth of 37 healthy piglets.

This work provides a promising first step in the development of genetic strategies for creating strains of pigs where the risk of transmission of retroviruses has been eliminated. It remains to be seen whether these results can be translated into a fully safe strategy in organ transplantation." Ian McConnell (University of Cambridge)

The eGenesis team are currently looking at further genetic modifications that can be made to increase the suitability of the organs for the human immune system.

Script:


V/O:
These piglets are special – not because they are cute, but because their genes have been altered to make them life savers par excellence.
George Church:
Each one of them could be saving 8 people from medical problems or more.
V/O:
Prof George Church is one of the world’s leading geneticists and molecular engineers, and works at Harvard University’s Medical School in the Unites States. He says it is quite feasible to use pig parts to save human lives because so much of pigs can be used for transplantation into humans.
George Church:
Almost every part of the pig, so the heart lungs, blood, kidney, liver, spleen, pancreas, various parts of the eye, skin…
LINK
Pig parts are very close to human organs both in size and basic physiology, and thus very suitable as replacement organs.
V/O:
For example, the heart on the left is a pig’s heart and the one on the right is a human heart. Hearts and many other porcine organs are almost identical to human organs. The idea to consider pig parts for transplantation into humans has been born out of necessity. There’s a severe worldwide shortage of life saving donor organs.

It is also the case in this country, says Samantha Nicholls of the Organ Donor Foundation in Cape Town.
Samantha:
There really is a dire need for more organ transplants in South Africa. Organ and tissue transplants. There are about 4300 adults awaiting transplants and less than 600 are performed each year.
LINK 2:
This number includes transplants of all organs as well as corneal transplants. These statistics clearly illustrate the dire need for transplant organs in South Africa.
V/O:
To further put it into perspective – South Africa has an exceptionally high rate of renal failure and because of this many thousands of people are in need of kidney transplants.
Samantha:
So, patients can be put on dialysis while they wait for a transplant. There are about 8000 people on dialysis on the country but that is not really a true reflection of how many people need a transplant. 50 000 people should on dialysis in the country.
V/O:
But what happens to those who cannot be accommodated in the system?
Samantha:
They are sent home to die. They are not dialysed, they are not treated. If organs were available, these patients lives would be saved and more space would be made on the waiting list so that further patients could be assisted and helped.
V/O:
And because of life style diseases, more and more people worldwide are in need of organ transplants every year.
LINK
Pigs have long been considered as a potential source for replacement organs, and in fact, pig heart valves like this one have been used for decades to replace human heart valves.
V/O:
And pig corneas are also regularly transplanted into human eyes.

But valves and corneas do not contain living cells and are much different from whole organs.

In the 1980’s a significant project was launched in the US to try and solve the need for replacement organs by attempting pig-to-human transplants. It cost upwards of 2 billion dollars, but was cancelled.
George Church:
And it was mainly shut down due to the presence of viruses in the pig cells that if released would infect the immune compromised patient and possible create a serious somatic disease similar of HIV, Ebola or swine flu.
V/O:
So, the presence of these viruses in the cells of pigs scuppered the project.

Over the last 20 years massive advances were made in the field of genomics and gene therapies and this proved to be a game changer in many medical fields.

Church himself has been at the forefront of groundbreaking genetic and genomic research and is responsible for the development of CRISPR-CAS9, the gene editing tool that has changed medicine profoundly the last few years. He is also part of the team working on the genome of the woolly mammoth to perhaps resurrecting it one day.
LINK:
Last year he was approached by transplant physicians who heard about his work to see if he could do anything about the viruses.
V/O:
There were 62 of these viruses.
Church:
These viruses are present in every cell of the pig, or every pig in the world. And it is not a matter that the pig is infected, the pig grows up, it develops from the egg with all these viruses and they are constantly being sluffed off and we have shown that the do infect human cells.
V/O:
So, Church and his team developed a gene editing procedure to edit the pig genome to remove the viruses from individual cells.
Church:
We were lucky because at the time people, none of us, including our lab that helped develop the technology had done more than one or two genes at a time. So, doing 62 was considered nearly impossible, and it turned out it was very easy to do. I mean, after 20 years of waiting and almost two-billion-dollar investment when it got shut down, we did it in a couple of weeks. It was very, very fast.
LINK 4
The technique they developed would create a strain of pig that has never existed before.
V/O:
The methodology is simple. They engineer the DNA of a cell to be virus free and implant this into an early stage embryo and as the embryo cells divide and proliferate, each and every cell that develops, does not have the viruses. The embryo eventually becomes a pig.
Church:
That pig will be free of the virus, and all of its offspring will be free of the virus. They will be different from any other pig in not having these viruses.
V/O:
This would make the pig organs disease free, but there is another serious problem in dealing with transplants -- rejection.

Even in cases where there is human to human transplants, the body will tend to reject foreign tissue and recipients of organs have to take immuno-suppressant drugs for life, to prevent rejection. The problem of rejection associated with inter-species transplants is even bigger.

But this presented no problem for Church – with the tools he has developed it is fairly simple to engineer a genome to have different properties and to create organs that would not be rejected by the human immune system.
Church:
There are a number of things you have to change in terms of the carbohydrate on the surface of the cells, some of the proteins involved in graph rejection and immune modulating proteins. All of those can be changed so that the pigs organs will not be rejected the way they would be from a regular pig.
LINK:
This is a massive breakthrough and right at the cutting edge of genomic engineering
Church:
Well, we are changing on the order of 62 genes for the viruses and in the order of 40 to50 genes for the carbohydrates and immune system and other blood factors. You are making cells that are not producing viruses and are acceptable to the human immune system.
V/O:
The first pigs free of viruses and compatible with humans, have already been born. What Church has achieved could alleviate the shortage of donor organs in a massive way - as it is cheap to raise pigs and it can be done almost everywhere, so organs don’t need to be transported over long distances - as is currently the case with human donor organs.
Church:
And eventually you will have a herd of pigs where they mate just like regular pigs. They don’t know that they are molecularly engineered and you don’t have to do molecular engineering every generation. You just have to do it once and you’re done., and then they grow just like regular pigs. Their offspring will forever be compatible with human transplants.
V/O:
But Church and his team are also doing more than just developing organs suitable for transplants. The research they are doing has staggering implications.
Church:
It will start to open our minds to preventative medicine much more. Much more radical preventative medicine. So each organ we transplant, we want it to be the best organ. The best and the cheapest. Which means we want it to be resistant to pathogens, we want it to be resistant to senescence and to cancer. And that is something that is hard to engineer a person to be resistant to pathogens, senescence and cancer, but the organs.. we are already manipulating the germline of the pig anyway, and with each generation of pig we can make it better and better so that in the end the organ might outlive the person.
V/O:
So their research also touches on genetic engineering to prevent organs from ageing. And techniques developed here could also perhaps make humans live much longer.
Church:
What you can do for organs, you can in principle do for the whole body. You practice on the organs until you are good at preventing ageing or reversing ageing, and then you can do it on a whole body. And that should not be limited to embryos. You should be able to do it at any age. And in fact, you can do it later on with gene therapy. I think we are going t see clinical trials on ageing reversal in animals and probably even in humans in the next five years.
V/O:
But for now they are looking at growing replacement organs. And for Samantha Nicholls the prospect of more transplant organs becoming available is good news.
Samantha:
If we can see an increase in the number of human organs available that would be the best option. But anything in medical advancement or scientific advancement that could assist and alleviate the number of patients on the waiting list, that is fantastic.
V/O:
But the big question with this breakthrough is: “How long will it take before a pig heart is beating in a human chest?”
Church:
I think this technology might be a year or two from curing people in clinical trials It will take another decade before it is broadly used throughout the entire population of people that can benefit from it.

Shortcomings in the law and widespread ignorance about organ donation are contributing to a major shortage of organs for transplant in South Africa. The problem is particularly severe among patients suffering from kidney failure, thousands of whom are turned away from the dialysis units of public hospitals every year. “Organ and tissue donation is not a priority for government and there is a huge need to spread the message about it in communities,” said Prof Magda Slabbert, an expert in medical law at Unisa’s College of Law, in a presentation on 1 March during the university’s annual Research & Innovation Week. Only two public hospitals in Gauteng were willing to provide statistics on the situation at their dialysis units, but their experience is illuminating, according to Slabbert. “They each show away approximately 500 patients a month. That’s 1 000 people who are shown the door per month and who actually go home to die because they cannot dialyse themselves.” Kidney failure is becoming chronic in South Africa, she said, mainly as a result of the growth in diabetes. Without access to dialysis or a kidney transplant, patients with kidney failure face a bleak future. And there are many thousands of people in dire need of other organs – heart, liver, pancreas, lung, etc. One way to fill the gap between need and supply would be to grow the organs another way — in animals. Scientists are now working to create designer pigs that could grow organs for human bodies. US scientists are the closest yet to creating genetically modified pigs with organs that can be safely transplanted into humans. The researchers identified and eliminated 25 porcine endogenous retroviruses (PERVS) hidden in the pigs’ DNA that can trigger organs to be rejected by the human immune system, thereby overcoming one of the biggest barriers in interspecies transplant or “xenotransplantation.” Our study highlighted the value of PERV inactivation to prevent cross-species viral transmission and demonstrated the successful production of PERV-inactivated animals to address the safety concern in clinical xenotransplantation,” Luhan Yang (Harvard university) and colleagues. The researchers say preventing the rejection of pig organs is a huge challenge, but that these pigs are the most genetically modified animals far. If xenotransplantation can be made safe, it has the potential to prevent the thousands of people in need of transplants having to wait so long to receive an organ. As reported in Science, the team used the gene-editing technology CRISPR to eliminate the viruses in 37 pigs. This game-changing technology involves a piece of “guide RNA” binding to a sequence of viral DNA and then guiding an enzyme to cut it at specific sites, so that DNA parts can be removed or added. Next, using the same cloning technology that created Dolly the sheep, the researchers inserted the modified genetic material into pigs’ eggs to create embryos, which resulted in the birth of 37 healthy piglets. This work provides a promising first step in the development of genetic strategies for creating strains of pigs where the risk of transmission of retroviruses has been eliminated. It remains to be seen whether these results can be translated into a fully safe strategy in organ transplantation." Ian McConnell (University of Cambridge) The eGenesis team are currently looking at further genetic modifications that can be made to increase the suitability of the organs for the human immune system.
